Threat of Terrorism, Increase of Presidential Power, and Economic Crisis (2001–2016)

options.misconception: Democrats and Republicans still dominate national elections today.
options.text: The end of the two-party system in national elections
Both parties competing harder for Hispanic voters in national elections

options.misconception: No such amendment exists; each citizen gets one vote.
options.text: A constitutional amendment giving new citizens extra votes

options.misconception: Immigration became more central to campaigns, not less.
options.text: The removal of immigration from presidential campaigns

rationales.A: Background: the two-party system survived the demographic change intact.
rationales.B: Background: as Hispanics grew to nearly a fifth of the population, their votes mattered more in close elections. Both parties began courting Hispanic voters openly.
rationales.C: Background: the Constitution gives every citizen one vote, and no amendment changed that.
rationales.D: Background: immigration stayed at the center of presidential campaigns, from 2016 onward.
rationales.general:
1. Turn the numbers into votes. Nearly a fifth of the population is a large voting bloc.
2. In close elections, a bloc that size can decide states, so parties chase it.
3. Background: the books note both parties openly courting Hispanic voters as the population grew.
4. The other choices describe changes that never happened: no third party takeover, no extra votes, no fading issue.
Remember: when a group grows, ask who wants its votes and why.
